Recovery of elemental sulphur from anaerobic efﬂuents through the biological
oxidation of sulphides
José Tavares de Sousa
, Jéssyca de Freitas Lima, Valquíria Cordeiro da Silva, Valderi Duarte Leite and Wilton
Silva Lopes
Departamento de Engenharia Sanitária e Ambiental, Programa de Pós-Graduação em Ciência e Tecnologia Ambiental, Universidade Estadual da
Paraiba, Campina Grande, Brazil
ABSTRACT
The aim of the present study was to evaluate the biological oxidation of sulphide in two different
UASB reactors by assessing the occurrence of oxidized forms of sulphur in the efﬂuents and the
amount of S0 that could be recovered in the process. The bioreactors employed were an
anaerobic hybrid (AH) reactor employing porous polyurethane foam as support media and a
micro-aerated UASB reactor equipped with an aeration device above the digestion zone. The AH
reactor produced a ﬁnal efﬂuent containing low concentrations of S2– (3.87% of total sulphur
load). It was achieved due to a complete oxidation of 56.1% of total sulphur. The partial
biological oxidation that occurred in the AH reactor allowed the recovery of 30% of the sulphur
load as S0. The efﬂuent from the micro-aerated UASB reactor contained 5% of the sulphur load
in the form of S2–, while 20.9% was present as dissolved SO4
2– and 46% was precipitated as S0. It
is concluded that the AH reactor or micro-aeration carried out above the digestion zone of the
UASB reactor favoured the biological oxidation of S2– and the release of odourless efﬂuents.
Both technologies represent feasible and low-cost alternatives for the anaerobic treatment of
domestic sewage.

Accepted 5 June 2016
KEYWORDS
Anaerobic system; sulphide
removal; elemental sulphur
recovery; odourless efﬂuents;
micro-aeration
1. Introduction
The upﬂow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reactor is an
attractive technology for the treatment of wastewaters
despite various limitations, which include the release of
gaseous emissions containing H2S.[1–3] This highly
toxic sulphide is produced when sulphate-reducing
bacteria present in the sludge bed obtain energy by
oxidizing organic compounds while reducing SO2−
4
to
H2S through dissimilatory sulphate reduction.[4] More-
over, the process of sulphidogenesis is harmful to
methanogenic archaea, and leads to a reduction in
the removal of chemical oxygen demand (COD) and a
diminution in the concentration of methane in the
biogas.[5–10]
The type of sulphide present in liquid waste during
biological treatment depends on pH, with volatile H2S
being the predominant form in the acid medium while
HS−and S2−are the principal species in neutral and alka-
line media, respectively.[11] Partial biological oxidation
of sulphide can occur in anaerobic, anoxic or aerobic
environments in which the electron acceptors are CO2,
NO−
3 or O2, respectively.[7] In anaerobic environments,
anoxygenic phototrophic bacteria, such as purple and
green sulphur bacteria, use energy from light to reduce
CO2 by transferring electrons from elemental sulphur
(S0).While purple bacteria store intracellular sulphur par-
ticles inside the cell and carry out complete oxidation to
SO2−
4 , green bacteria deposit sulphur granules outside
the cell and perform incomplete oxidation.[12] It is note-
worthy, however, that partial as well as complete oxi-
dation of sulphides can occur with both groups of
bacteria. In this context, Garcia et al. [2] reported that
cyanobacteria (Phormidium and Pseudoanabaena) and
sulphur-oxidizing bacteria similar to Beggiatoa or Thiotrix,
present in the scum layer of the settler compartment of a
UASB reactor, reduced sulphide concentration sand
could play a role in minimizing odour emission.
The supply of oxygen at low concentrations may
remove the main product of sulphide oxidation, that is,
insoluble elemental sulphur, from the liquid phase.[13]
The presence of small quantities of oxygen, about
0.1 mgO2 L−1, in anaerobic reactors is sufﬁcient to
create micro-aerobic conditions that enable microbial
communities to partially oxidize sulphide to S0, accord-
ing to Equation (1):[13–17]
HS−+ 1 2O2  S0 + OH−.

Van der Zee et al. [18] studied the fate of sulphur com-
pounds and oxygen during micro-aerobic sulphide oxi-
dation and found that the introduction of a low air ﬂow
of 0.7–0.9 m3 m−3 reactor volume day−1 (corresponding
to an O2/S molar ratio of 8–10) to a ﬂuidized bed reactor
was sufﬁcient to reduce the H2S content in the biogas to
levels that were almost undetectable (∼0.02%).[5]
Application of micro-aerobic UASB as an alternative
technology would not only assist in solving the
problem of odour emission but would also allow the
recovery of S0 present in sewage. The elemental
sulphur so recovered could be employed in the indus-
trial production of H2SO4 or (NH4)2SO4 for use in agricul-
ture,
thus
adding
extra
value
to
the
treatment
process.[19,20]
Considering the problems of sulphide formation in
anaerobic reactors, the present study aimed (i) to evalu-
ate the performance of two different UASB reactors in
the treatment of domestic wastewater by assessing the
occurrence of oxidized forms of sulphur (S0 and SO2−
4 )
in the efﬂuents and (ii) to estimate the amount of S0
recovered in the processes. The bioreactors employed
were an anaerobic hybrid (AH) reactor comprising
porous polyurethane foam as support media and a
micro-aerated UASB reactor equipped with an aeration
device above the digestion zone.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Site of study and origin of sewage
The experiments were carried out at the Estação Exper-
imental de Tratamento Biológico de Esgotos Sanitários
(EXTRABES) located in an area belonging to the Compan-
hia de Água e Esgotos da Paraíba (CAGEPA) and the Uni-
versidade Estadual da Paraiba, Campina Grande, PB,
Brazil (7°14′24′′ S; 35°53′02′′ W; 550 m altitude). The
municipal wastewaters employed in the experiments
were collected using a submersible pump installed in
an inspection well of the CAGEPA east sewer interceptor
pipe. The sewage ﬂowed by gravity through 2 cm diam-
eter plastic tubing to an equalization tank (100 L)
equipped with a peristaltic metering pump with preset
ﬂow system to feed the reactor.
2.2. Characteristics and operational conditions of
the anaerobic reactors
The AH reactor was constructed from polyvinyl chloride
(PVC) tubing (2 m × 20 cm diameter) and comprised a
UASB unit of useful volume 27 L operating with a hydrau-
lic retention time (HRT) of 6 h, and an anaerobic ﬁlter of
useful volume 25 L operating with an HRT of 5:30 h. The
anaerobic ﬁlter support consisted of polyurethane
sponge cubes (3 × 3 × 3 cm) that occupied 70 cm of the
ﬁlter height and presented 97% void volume. The raw
sewage (inﬂuent) entered the UASB unit at the base
and moved with a continuous ascendant ﬂow provided
by the peristaltic pump. A tap was provided at the top
of the UASB unit for the collection of efﬂuent samples,
and the ﬁnal treated efﬂuent was collected with the
aid of another tap located above the anaerobic ﬁlter.
The growth of dispersed and adherent sludge in the
UASB and ﬁlter units, respectively, could be monitored
in samples collected using further 10 taps spaced
throughout the reactor body. A schematic of the AH
system projected for a bench-scale experiment is pre-
sented in Figure 1(a), and the physical and operational
parameters are given in Table 1. The complete reactor
presented a useful volume of 52 L, operated with a
total HRT of 11:30 h and had a sewage treatment
capacity of 108 L day−1. The inoculum used in starting
the system was anaerobic sewage (6.5 L) with biomass
containing 48 g L−1 of total solids and 28 g L−1 of total
volatile solids. The reactor was monitored over a six-
month operational period. During this period samples
of 100 mL of the efﬂuents were collected weekly (24
samples) on Wednesdays at 8 a.m. in both reactors. In
the micro-aerated UASB reactor, monthly samples of
sludge were collected (500 mL) for determination of
sulphur species.
The micro-aerated UASB reactor (Figure 1(b)) was
constructed from PVC tubing (2 m × 20 cm diameter)
and presented a useful volume of 25 L, of which 17 L
(68%) was micro-aerated and 8 L (32%) corresponded
to the digestion zone. Sewage entered at the base of
the reactor, and the treatment capacity of the reactor
was 50 L day−1. The rationale behind the reactor oper-
ation was to supply a low ﬂow of oxygen to permit
the oxidation of sulphur species produced by sul-
phate-reducing
bacteria
during
sulphidogenesis,
thereby
yielding
an
odourless
efﬂuent.
Hence,
a
micro-aeration module with 3.5 L useful volume was
connected to the main body of the reactor at point 1
(Figure 1(b)) with the base of the unit located 20 cm
below the efﬂuent outlet of the main reactor. The
module contained a porous stone sparger and was con-
nected to a nebulizer (Nebular Plus®, Daru, Inhauma, RJ,
Brazil) so that a fraction of the UASB efﬂuent could be
aerated and returned through a PVC tube (4 mm diam-
eter) that entered the main reactor at point 2 (Figure 1
(b)) located 46 cm above the reactor base. The airﬂow
injected daily was monitored using a gas meter (Lao
Indústria, Osasco, SP, Brazil) connected to a ﬂow
meter (Oxigel, São Paulo, SP, Brazil) measuring in the
range of 0–1.5 L min−1. The concentration of dissolved

daily with the aid of an Oakton Instruments (Vernon
Hills, IL, USA) model DO 6 economy handheld dissolved
oxygen meter. The level of dissolved oxygen was veri-
ﬁed on a weekly basis using a Beluga-type biogas respi-

Paraiba) attached to a YSI (Yellow Springs, OH, USA)
electrode and the readings were recorded and plotted
in spreadsheet form.[21] The reactor was monitored
over a three-month operational period.
2.3. Analysis of raw sewage and reactor efﬂuents
The standard methods described by the APHA/AWWA/
WEF [22] were employed to assess COD (titrimetric
closed reﬂux; APHA/AWWA/WEF section 5220C), sul-
phide
(methylene
blue
method;
APHA/AWWA/WEF
section 4500D) and pH (potentiometry). Alkalinity (mg
CaCO3L−1) was determined using the Kapp method
according to Buchauer,[23] while elemental sulphur
was measured colorimetrically using the method of Bar-
tlett and Skoog.[24] The concentrations of SO2−
4
present
were analysed by ion chromatography using a Dionex™
model ICS-1100 chromatograph with suppressed and
detector conductivity (Thermo Scientiﬁc, Waltham, MA,
USA). The mobile phase was carbonate 4.5 and 0.8 mM
bicarbonate. The column (2 × 250 mm) with a particle
size of 6.0 µm, capacity column80 μeq/column functional
group alkyl/alkanol quaternary ammonium, hydrophobi-
city low was used. Efﬂuent samples were submitted to
two consecutive ﬁltrations through cellulose acetate
membranes (0.45 and 0.22 µm) and then diluted ﬁve
times prior to analysis. Scanning electron microscopy
with energy-dispersive X-ray (SEM/EDX) was performed
using a TM-1000 bench model instrument (Hitachi,
Tokyo, Japan) to observe submicron-scale features of
the solid material precipitated in the anaerobic ﬁlter
efﬂuent and to provide elemental identiﬁcation and
quantitative compositional information. Samples were
analysed without prior application of conductive metal
coating at a magniﬁcation of up 10,000×, depth of
focus
of
1 mm,
resolution
of
30 nm,
acceleration
voltage of 15 kV and low vacuum with variable pressure
between 1 and 270 Pa. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of
the samples was performed using an XRD-7000 diffract-
ometer (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) and scanned in the
Bragg-Brentano mode with a scattering angle 2θ of 5–
80°, geometry of θ-2θ, Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54 Å), step
size 0.02° (2θ steps) , and interval of 0.5 s.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performance of the AH reactor
The chemical characteristics of the raw sewage supplied
to the AH reactor and efﬂuents derived from the UASB
and the anaerobic ﬁlter are given in Table 2. The mean
pH values of raw sewage and UASB efﬂuents varied
between 7.7 and 7.4 with a standard deviation ≤0.30,
which is considered substantial taking into account the
inﬂuence of pH on the competition between sulphate-
reducing bacteria and methanogenic archaea. Visser
et al. [25] demonstrated that the efﬁciency of sulphate
removal by a UASB reactor is a function of the pH of
the efﬂuent, in that the reduction of SO2−
4
predominates
when the pH is higher than 8 but the production of
methane and the reduction of SO2−
4
are in equilibrium
when the pH varies between 6.75 and 7.5. In the
present study, it is likely that the high alkalinity values
(determined as mg CaCO3 L−1) of the raw sewage and
the reactor efﬂuents enhanced the buffering efﬁciency
of the system and accounted for the relatively small vari-
ations in pH.
The concentrations of S2−and SO2−
4 in the raw sewage
fed to the AH reactor were, respectively, 7.77 and
14.43 mg L−1 corresponding to a total sulphur load in
the inﬂuent of 22.2 mg L−1, whereas the total concen-
tration
of
sulphur
in
the
UASB
efﬂuent
was
20.59 mg L−1
indicating
a
loss
of
approximately
1.61 mg L−1 (Table 2). In contrast, the total concentration
of the studied anions in the efﬂuent from the anaerobic
ﬁlter was around 13.32 mg L−1, and they were present
mainly in the form of SO2−
4
(12.46 mg L−1) rather than
S2−(0.86 mg L−1). During the experiment, the top of the
anaerobic ﬁlter was open to the air, thus permitting
gaseous exchange and the ingress of light. Under these
conditions, the S2−species produced in the UASB unit
were oxidized to SO2−
4
and S0, as has been observed in
previous studies.[2,7,26,27]
The marked increase in the concentration of S2−in the
UASB efﬂuent compared with that in the raw sewage was
probably due to containment of the inﬂuent in the equal-
ization tank, which promoted the occurrence of sulphido-
genesis prior to entry into the UASB reactor. Indeed, the
concentration of S2−in the UASB efﬂuent remained high
during the whole experiment, demonstrating the efﬁ-
ciency of sulphate-reducing bacteria in transforming
SO2−
4
to S2−. Oxidation of S2−in the anaerobic ﬁlter unit
was mediated by suspended cells of photoautotrophic
and/or photoheterotrophic bacteria containing chloro-
phyll and carotenoid pigments. These organisms were
able to survive in such an environment because the top
of the ﬁlter unit was open to the air and exposed to
light.[27,28] As a consequence of this activity, the efﬂuent
from the anaerobic ﬁlter exhibited a low concentration of
S2−(0.86 mg L−1) and the unpleasant odour that is typical
of anaerobic efﬂuents was substantially reduced. On the
other hand, the concentration of SO2−
4
remained high,
thus maintaining the complete oxidation of S2−to SO2−
4 .
It is likely that the population of purple bacteria predomi-
nated under the prevailing experimental conditions,
thereby favouring complete oxidation to SO2−
4 .[12]

The
quantitative
analysis
revealed
that
30%
(6.66 mg L−1) of the sulphur load present in the raw
sewage was recovered as elemental sulphur, while the
XRD pattern of the solid material that precipitated from
the anaerobic ﬁlter efﬂuent (Figure 2(a)) conﬁrmed the
predominant presence of S0. Figure 2(b) presents a
SEM image of the surface of this solid material at
1200 × ampliﬁcation, while the energy-dispersive X-ray
(EDX) spectrum, shown in Figure 2(c), displayed only
the characteristic peak of elemental sulphur, thereby
conﬁrming that 98% of the precipitate present in the
anaerobic ﬁlter efﬂuent was actually S0. Silva et al. [29]
also reported that areas of a UASB reactor exposed to
light supported the growth of bacterial populations
employing S2−as electron donor in energy-producing
processes and forming insoluble precipitates containing
87% of S0. In the present study, the total concentration of
sulphur in the inﬂuent was 22.2 mg L−1, whereas the
ﬁnal anaerobic efﬂuent contained 19.98 mg L−1 of the
element when all of the chemical species analysed (i.e.
SO2−
4 , S2−and S0) were taken into account. It was not
possible to determine the fate of the residual portion
of the sulphur load, but it was probably discharged in
the volatile form (H2S) or remained undetected in the
sediment.
3.2. Performance of the micro-aerated UASB
reactor
The chemical characteristics of the raw sewage supplied
to the micro-aerated UASB reactor and the efﬂuent
derived the reform are given in Table 3. The mean pH
values of raw sewage and efﬂuent (7.91 and 7.75,
respectively), although slightly above the preferred
range of 7.0–7.5, were acceptable given that values
below 6.5 and above 8.5 are inhibitory to methanogenic
archaea.[30] However, it is important to maintain pH at
around 7.0 when attempting to remove sulphides,
since in this region 50% of the sulphur species are disso-
ciated (HS–) and 50% are in the non-dissociated and
more toxic form (H2S).[31] As for the AH reactor, the
high alkalinity values of the raw sewage and the UASB
efﬂuent enhanced the buffering capacity of the system,
resulting in minimal variations in pH.
The concentrations of S2−and SO2−
4 in the raw sewage
fed to the micro-aerated UASB reactor were 2.36 and
7.68 mg L−1, respectively, corresponding to a total con-
centration of sulphur in the inﬂuent of 10.04 mg
L−1(Table 3). In the UASB efﬂuent, the concentrations
of S2−and SO2−
4
were considerably lower (at 0.5 and
2.1 mg L−1, respectively), indicating that only 5% of the
inﬂuent sulphur was converted into sulphide. In contrast,
4.62 mg L−1 of elemental sulphur was recovered from
the UASB efﬂuent, representing 46% of the sulphur
load in the raw sewage, thereby conﬁrming that micro-
aeration applied above the reaction zone of the UASB
reactor favoured the partial oxidation of sulphide
species, as previously reported.[32] Under aerobic con-
ditions, oxygen serves as an electron acceptor in the oxi-
dation
of
sulphide
by
chemolithotrophic
bacteria,
[14,33,34] especially those of the genus Thiobacillus
that display a great afﬁnity for sulphur compounds.
Under limiting oxygen conditions, the formation of S0 is
favoured, while increased oxygen concentration promotes
the production of SO2−
4 , [35,36] thereby contributing to
the undesirable complete oxidation of S2−to SO2−
4 .

3.3. Mass balance of sulphur in the micro-aerated
UASB reactor
In order to understand the behaviour of sulphur species
in the micro-aerated UASB reactor, the mean concen-
trations of sulphur forms with oxidation state +6 and
–2 were assessed. The levels of dissolved SO2−
4
and S2−
in the liquid phase were determined in the inﬂuent
(raw
sewage),
efﬂuent
and
sludge
according
to
Equations (2)–(4), and the results are presented in
Figure 3. Of the total sulphur load present in the inﬂuent
(502 mgS day−1), 20.9% (105 mgS day−1) of SO2−
4
and
4.98% (25 mgS day−1) of S2−remained dissolved in the
efﬂuent, while 46% (231 mgS day−1) was recovered
from the efﬂuent as insoluble S0. Considering that
11.12% of the total sulphur load was found in the
sludge (55.85 mgS day−1), it is likely that the residual
16.96% represents the volume of H2S produced by the
UASB reactor which, under the experimental conditions
employed (30°C and 0.95 atm), would amount to
77 mL day−1.
According to Speece,[37] it is very difﬁcult to close the
mass balance of sulphur for an anaerobic process owing
to the problem of sulphide conversion, which may be
caused by the microbial synthesis of sulphur resulting
in the internal precipitation of sulphide produced. The
discrepancy observed in the experimental data obtained
in the present study can be explained by the different
pathways of conversion of dissolved SO2−
4
and S2−in
the UASB reactor. For example, SO2−
4 can be reduced to
S2−for the formation of organic compounds through an
assimilatory route or for the production of energy by a
dissimilation pathway. In the latter case, the S2−is
excreted into the medium where it may precipitate
through combining with a metal and accumulate in the
sludge in the form of acid volatile sulphides [22,38]
that can be used as a source of energy, [39] or be
released in the gas phase (H2S stripping). Another impor-
tant consideration is that a portion of the sulphur, theor-
etically immobilized as bioparticles in the sludge, may
actually be carried away in the efﬂuent and, therefore,
not measured. In a recent study of the mass balance of
sulphur in a UASB reactor fed with raw sewage, Souza
[40] reported that 15–18% of the original sulphur load
was present as SO2−
4
in the efﬂuent, 57–64% as S2−in
the efﬂuent, 3–5% as S2−precipitated in the retained

3.4. Oxygen ﬂow in the micro-aerated UASB
reactor
In the absence of homogenization, the concentration of
dissolved oxygen determined above the digestion zone
oscillated between cycles and the values obtained
were not reproducible. However, since the airﬂow was
maintained at a mean value of 1.2 ± 0.39 L h−1, and con-
sidering that the speciﬁc mass of air is 1.2 g L−1 while the
oxygen fraction in air is 23.3% (w/w), the amount of
oxygen supplied to the micro-aeration unit was in the
region of 334 mg h−1 or 10.44 mmol h−1. Micro-aeration
during the trial period ensured a constant concentration
of dissolved oxygen around 0.46 ± 0.088 mg L−1, permit-
ting the conversion of sulphur species into the most oxi-
dized
forms,
such
as
SO2−
4
and
S0.
The
oxygen
consumption rate above the aeration zone was 0.70 ±
0.14 mgO2 L−1 h−1, a value that was about 70 times
lower than that of the conventional activated sludge
process.[43] The ﬂow rate of the raw sewage in the
UASB reactor employed in the present study was
2.08 L h−1 and the total sulphur load was 10.04 mg L−1,
hence the sulphur ﬂow rate was 20.88 mg h−1 or
0.65 mmol h−1 giving a mmolO2/mmolS rate ratio of
approximately16.0 mmol h−1.Van der Zee et al. [18]
obtained mmolO2/mmolS ratios of between 8 and
10 mmol h−1 in a micro-aerated anaerobic reactor, and
found that these levels were sufﬁcient to ensure that
the amount of sulphide in the biogas was reduced to
concentrations
of
approximately
0.02%.
Moreover,
these authors reported that such molar ratios favoured
the oxidation of S2−to S0, S2O3
2−and, most likely, polysul-
phides, by routes that did not involve the re-oxidation of
reduced sulphur species to SO2−
4 .
According to Jansen et al., [13] signiﬁcant amounts of
thiosulphate are formed when the O2/S ratio in a reactor
is below 0.7, for example, indicating that the chemical
oxidation of S2−to S2O3
2 is favoured under limiting
oxygen conditions. In the present study, the biological
oxidation of S2−followed ﬁrst-order reaction kinetics (k
= 0.28–0.47 h−1) during the 120 days of operation of
the system. However, the chemical oxidation of S2−
could also be described as a ﬁrst-order reaction (k =
0.87 h−1) and it is likely, therefore, that the system
would have a lower capacity to perform biological oxi-
dations in comparison with chemical oxidations under
limiting oxygen conditions. On the other hand, under
limiting S2−conditions, the oxidation of S2−by chemo-
lithotrophic Thiobacillus is favoured in comparison with
chemical oxidation by virtue of the strong afﬁnity of
these microorganisms for sulphur.[36] The complete oxi-
dation of S2−to SO2−
4
by colourless sulphur bacteria gen-
erates more useful metabolic energy than partial
oxidation. In order to obtain partial oxidation, it would
be necessary to supply high sulphur loads or low
oxygen concentrations.[44]
In the present study, the effects of micro-aeration on
the removal of COD from the ﬁnal efﬂuent were not
investigated although the O2/COD ratio in the reactor
was estimated to be 0.027 (cf. Table 3). In this context,
Van der Zee et al. [18] reported that the removal of
COD was insigniﬁcant when the O2/COD ratio was
around 0.05.
4. Conclusions
The AH reactor not only removed a considerable frac-
tion of organic material (77%) but also produced a
ﬁnal efﬂuent with a low concentration of S2−(3.87%
of the total sulphur load), resulting in a signiﬁcant
reduction in the unpleasant odour typical of anaerobic
efﬂuents. It was achieved due to a complete oxidation
of S2−to SO2−
4
(56.1% of the total sulphur load)
carried out, most probably, by anoxygenic purple and
green bacteria. The partial biological oxidation that
occurred in the AH reactor allowed the recovery of
30% of the sulphur load as S0. Regarding the micro-
aerated UASB reactor, only 4.98% of the sulphur load
was released in the efﬂuent as S2−, whereas 20.9%
was present in the form of dissolved SO2−
4
and 46%
was precipitated in the form of S0. A small amount of
S0 (2.32%) was also found in the sludge. Thus, anaerobic
ﬁltration or micro-aeration carried out above the diges-
tion zone of a UASB reactor favoured the biological oxi-
dation of S2−and the release of relatively odourless
efﬂuents. Both technologies represent feasible and
low-cost alternatives for the anaerobic treatment of
domestic sewage.
